The rule cites the Google title-link doc as SPEC for numeric thresholds the doc does not contain; the doc's actual guidance is qualitative ('descriptive and concise', avoid keyword stuffing and boilerplate).
The missing-title 'error' path duplicates head-title's error for the same condition (intentional granular split, but the double error is redundant noise).

When the title is missing, return a neutral/info result deferring to head-title's existing error.

rules.description: Checks for head > meta[charset], warns when absent or empty, ok for UTF-8, info for any other value.

Understated severity for non-UTF-8: the fetched WHATWG spec requires 'its value must be an ASCII case-insensitive match for the string "utf-8"' - any other charset value is non-conforming HTML, yet the rule reports it as mere 'info' with '(Recommend UTF-8)'. It should be at least 'warn'.
The cited SPEC is MDN (secondary source); the normative source is the WHATWG HTML standard.
rules.proposedFix: Also inspect meta[http-equiv=Content-Type i] and the response Content-Type header charset before warning about a missing declaration; raise non-UTF-8 values from 'info' to 'warn' citing the WHATWG utf-8 requirement; replace the MDN reference with https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/semantics.html#attr-meta-charset.
rules.skepticNote: confirmed: I could not refute the claim; every point checks out against the code and the fetched WHATWG text. (1) False-positive risk is real: /Users/franzenzenhofer/dev/franz-enzenhofer-seo-live-test-v7/v7/src/rules/head/metaCharset.ts queries only `head > meta[charset]` and on absence emits type 'warn' with "Missing <meta charset> declaration.", but the WHATWG standard (https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/semantics.html#charset) says verbatim: "If an HTML document does not start with a BOM, and its encoding is not explicitly given by Content-Type metadata, and the document is not an iframe srcdoc document, then the encoding must be specified using a meta element with a charset attribute or a meta element with an http-equiv attribute in the Encoding declaration state" - so a page declaring encoding via BOM, the Content-Type header, or meta http-equiv is conforming yet gets warned. (2) Understated severity is also spec-backed: the spec states "If the attribute is present, its value must be an ASCII case-insensitive match for the string 'utf-8'" and "Regardless of whether a character encoding declaration is present or not, the actual character encoding used to encode the document must be UTF-8. [ENCODING]" - a "must"-level conformance violation, which the rule downgrades to type 'info' with "(Recommend UTF-8)". (3) The SPEC constant in the rule is indeed the MDN URL (https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Element/meta#charset), a secondary source, while the normative requirement lives in the WHATWG standard. The proposed fix (check http-equiv and the response Content-Type header before warning, raise non-UTF-8 to warn, cite WHATWG) matches the spec; the only nuance is that BOM detection may not be possible from the parsed DOM alone, but that does not invalidate the finding.

rules.description: Checks the rel=canonical link element: presence, uniqueness, in-<head> placement, non-empty href, no fragment, absolute URL, and whether it self-references the page URL.

Individual checks are spec-grounded: multiple canonicals (RFC 6596: 'Specify only one canonical link relation for a resource'), outside-<head> ('The rel=canonical link element is only accepted if it appears in the <head> section'), relative URL warn ('we don't recommend them'), fragment warn ('Google Search generally doesn't support URL fragments').

The sibling head:canonical-tracking-params rule only checks a fixed tracking-param list and does not mitigate this. The reviewer's other assertions check out verbatim against the spec ("only accepted if it appears in the <head> section", absolute paths recommended over relative, fragments unsupported; RFC 6596 mandates a single canonical relation), and the proposed fix (keep the query string in the self-reference comparison, or strip only known tracking params, and report same-path-different-query as "points to") is sound.

rules.description: Parses the HTTP Link header for rel=canonical: info when absent, ok for exactly one, error for multiple header canonicals.

Parser deduplicates identical URLs before counting, so only genuinely different duplicates error. Note the multiple-header error is also re-implemented inside head:canonical-signals-conflict.

rules.description: Compares HTML link canonical against HTTP header canonical: error when both are set (matching or not), error on multiple header canonicals.

Google explicitly says both methods together are 'supported' - merely 'more error prone' ('while supported, using both methods at the same time is more error prone') - so a matching pair is a recommendation-level issue, not an error.
The genuinely-different case is correctly an error ('Don't specify different URLs as canonical for the same page using different canonicalization techniques').
The multiple-header-canonicals error duplicates the identical check in head:canonical-header (same parseHeaderCanonicals input, same verdict), producing double findings for one defect.

rules.skepticNote: confirmed: Refutation fails on all three points. (1) The code (src/rules/head/canonicalSignalsConflict.ts) returns type: 'error' even when normalizedHtml === normalizedHeader ("Both HTML and HTTP canonicals set; remove one source to avoid conflicts.", priority 150) - the `matches` flag only changes message and priority, not type. Google's spec (https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/consolidate-duplicate-urls) says verbatim: "We recommend that you choose one of these and go with that; while supported, using both methods at the same time is more error prone" - i.e. a matching pair is explicitly supported and only recommendation-level, so 'error' is a misclassification and 'warn'/'info' with the choose-one recommendation is correct. (2) The differing-URLs case correctly stays 'error': the spec says "Don't specify different URLs as canonical for the same page using different canonicalization techniques". (3) The multiple-header check is genuinely duplicated: both canonicalSignalsConflict.ts and canonicalHeader.ts (head:canonical-header) run parseHeaderCanonicals(linkHeaderOf(page.headers)) and each emits its own 'error' when length > 1; the rule `what` field ('static' vs 'http') is used only for timeouts/metadata in src/core/ruleTimeouts.ts and runHelpers.ts, not for gating, so both rules fire on the same page and a single defect yields double findings. RFC 6596 adds nothing contrary (it defines the relation, silent on multi-source conflicts). The reviewer's claim stands.

rules.description: Errors when an HTTPS page declares an HTTP canonical (HTTPS-to-HTTP downgrade); ok otherwise.
issues: Directly backed: Google 'prefers HTTPS pages over equivalent HTTP pages as canonical' and explicitly lists 'The HTTPS page has a rel=canonical link to the HTTP page' as a condition that breaks HTTPS preference; the documented fix is 'Add a rel=canonical link from the HTTP page to the HTTPS page'. Error severity is justified since the annotation actively defeats a documented Google preference.

rules.description: Warns when the canonical URL contains known tracking parameters (utm_*, gclid, fbclid, msclkid, etc., extensible via config); also warns on non-http(s) canonical schemes.
issues: No Google doc names tracking parameters in canonicals specifically, but the principle is supported: the canonical is the 'preferred' URL of a duplicate set, and Google's URL-structure guidance says 'shorten URLs by trimming unnecessary parameters (meaning, parameters that don't change the content)' - which tracking params by definition are. The specific param list is an industry heuristic, hence 'general' provenance; 'warn' severity is appropriate. Non-http(s)-scheme warn is a sound sanity check.

rules.description: Compares the canonical URL to the observed navigation/redirect chain: warns when the canonical equals a URL that redirected, or when the canonical differs from the final landing URL.
issues: The canonical-points-to-a-redirecting-URL warn is well grounded (Google: 'Any content Google receives from the redirecting URL is ignored, and the final target URL's content is processed instead'; permanent redirects signal 'the redirect target should be canonical').

The blanket 'Canonical URL differs from final landing URL... Align them to avoid conflicting signals' warn contradicts the documented purpose of rel=canonical: pointing a duplicate page to a DIFFERENT preferred URL is exactly the supported use case in consolidate-duplicate-urls, not a conflicting signal. This case also duplicates head-canonical's non-self-reference reporting, so the same legitimate situation is flagged twice.
Uses the same query-stripping normalizeUrl as head-canonical, so ?param differences are silently equated.
rules.proposedFix: Keep the redirecting-canonical warn; downgrade the plain canonical-differs-from-final-URL case to info/neutral (it is legitimate canonicalization) unless the canonical target itself is known to redirect or the difference is only scheme/host of the same page.
rules.skepticNote: confirmed: Not refuted - the reviewer's claim checks out against both the code and the spec. In /Users/franzenzenhofer/dev/franz-enzenhofer-seo-live-test-v7/v7/src/rules/head/canonicalNavConsistency.ts the final `if (normCanonical !== normFinal)` branch returns type 'warn' (priority 220) with "Canonical URL (...) differs from final landing URL (...). Align them to avoid conflicting signals." for ANY non-matching canonical, even with zero redirects observed. Google's consolidate-duplicate-urls doc (https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/consolidate-duplicate-urls) defines rel=canonical as "an element used in the head section of HTML to indicate that another page is representative of the content on the page" - i.e. pointing a duplicate page at a DIFFERENT preferred URL is the documented purpose, not a conflicting signal; self-referential canonicals are only "recommend[ed]", not required. The duplication claim also holds: src/rules/head/canonical.ts (head-canonical) already emits a 'warn' (priority 500, "Canonical points to <url>.") for the same non-self-referencing case, so the legitimate situation is flagged twice. And the shared normalizeUrl in src/shared/url-utils.ts sets `u.search = ''`, silently equating ?param variants exactly as claimed. The redirecting-canonical warn the reviewer keeps is consistent with Google's redirect guidance (permanent redirects signal the target should be canonical), so the proposed fix - keep the redirect warn, downgrade the plain differs-from-final case to info/neutral - is well grounded.

rules.description: Warns when the hreflang cluster omits the canonical URL or when hreflang alternates use a different host, or HTTP where the canonical is HTTPS.
issues: Canonical-in-cluster check is supported (localized-versions: 'Each language version must list itself as well as all other language versions') and the HTTPS check is supported (consolidate doc: 'Don't include the HTTP version of your pages in your sitemap or hreflang annotations').

The same-host requirement is NOT spec-supported: the rule counts every hreflang alternate on a different host as a mismatch ('url.host === canonicalHost' gate), but Google requires only fully-qualified URLs ('Alternate URLs must be fully-qualified, including the transport method') and nothing in localized-versions restricts alternates to one host - multi-ccTLD setups (example.de / example.fr) are a normal localized-site architecture and would be falsely warned as 'misaligned with canonical URL'.
rules.proposedFix: Drop the host-equality mismatch condition (or reduce it to info); keep the HTTP-vs-HTTPS mismatch and the canonical-in-cluster check as the warn conditions.
rules.skepticNote: confirmed: The reviewer's issue is confirmed, not refuted. The rule (v7/src/rules/head/canonicalHreflangConsistency.ts, line 50) skips an alternate only when `url.host === canonicalHost && (!canonicalHttps || url.protocol === 'https:')`, so every hreflang alternate on a different host increments mismatchCount and triggers the warn "Hreflang cluster is misaligned with canonical URL" (lines 60-78). But the cited spec, https://developers.google.com/search/docs/specialty/international/localized-versions, states verbatim in its "Guidelines for all methods" section: "Alternate URLs do not need to be in the same domain." (verified in the raw page text, immediately after "Alternate URLs must be fully-qualified, including the transport method (http/https)"). Cross-domain hreflang (example.de / example.fr) is thus explicitly permitted by Google, and the rule's host-equality condition would falsely warn on a compliant multi-ccTLD setup. The reviewer's other two claims also hold: the canonical-in-cluster check matches "Each language version must list itself as well as all other language versions" (same page), and the HTTPS concern is supported by https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/consolidate-duplicate-urls ("Don't include the HTTP version of your pages in your sitemap or hreflang annotations"). The proposed fix (drop or downgrade the host-equality condition, keep the HTTP-vs-HTTPS and canonical-in-cluster warn conditions) is correct per spec.

rules.description: Warns when a canonical (HTML or HTTP header) coexists with noindex (meta robots or X-Robots-Tag) - conflicting signals.
issues: The conflict itself is defensible from Google's docs (consolidate doc: 'We don't recommend using noindex to prevent selection of a canonical page within a single site... rel=canonical link annotations are the preferred solution'), and warn is the right severity.

Detection gaps: the selector 'head > meta[name="robots"]' matches the name attribute case-sensitively ('name' is not in HTML's case-insensitive attribute-matching list), so <meta name="Robots" content="noindex"> is missed although Google treats meta names case-insensitively; a <meta name="googlebot" content="noindex"> is missed entirely ('Any rule that can be used in a robots meta tag can also be specified as an X-Robots-Tag', and googlebot-scoped metas carry the same rules); and a user-agent-scoped X-Robots-Tag like 'googlebot: noindex' fails the token comparison because the token is 'googlebot: noindex', not 'noindex'.
rules.proposedFix: Use meta[name="robots" i] plus meta[name="googlebot" i], and strip optional user-agent prefixes from X-Robots-Tag values before tokenizing.
rules.skepticNote: confirmed: The reviewer is correct on every point. (1) Case-sensitivity: the rule (src/rules/head/canonicalNoindexConflict.ts, line `page.doc.querySelector('head > meta[name="robots"]')`) matches the name attribute value case-sensitively — HTML spec 4.16.2 "Case-sensitivity of selectors" (https://html.spec.whatwg.org/multipage/semantics-other.html) lists the attributes whose values are matched ASCII case-insensitively (accept, charset, rel, type, ...) and "name" is not among them — while Google's robots-meta-tag doc states "Both the name and the content attributes are case-insensitive", so `<meta name="Robots" content="noindex">` is indeed missed (content case is fine since parseTokens lowercases). (2) The code queries only name="robots", but Google's doc explicitly supports crawler-scoped metas ("to address a specific crawler, replace the robots value of the name attribute with the user agent token", example `<meta name="googlebot" content="nosnippet">`), so `<meta name="googlebot" content="noindex">` is missed. (3) parseTokens splits only on [,;], so a header per Google's documented form ("The X-Robots-Tag may optionally specify a user agent before the rules", example `X-Robots-Tag: googlebot: nofollow`) yields the token "googlebot: noindex", which fails the exact `.includes('noindex')` comparison. The proposed fix (meta[name="robots" i] + meta[name="googlebot" i], strip user-agent prefixes before tokenizing) directly addresses these; the conflict premise and warn severity are also supported by the consolidate-duplicate-urls doc.

rules.description: Evaluates www/non-www host canonicalization from the observed navigation: expects a single permanent (301/308) server redirect preserving path+query; errors on client-side redirects, temporary redirects, multi-hop chains, and canonical-only host resolution.
issues: Well supported parts: permanent redirects are the strong canonical signal ('the indexing pipeline uses the redirect as a signal that the redirect target should be canonical', 302/307 'doesn't use the redirect as a signal'), and JS redirects are last-resort ('Only use JavaScript redirects if you can't do server-side or meta refresh redirects'), so erroring on client redirects and temporary redirects for host canonicalization is defensible.
